subject: Vocabulary
description: Common homophones (sound-alike, different meaning); SSC PYQ favourites

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'I appreciate your ___ counsel.' (advice / advise)

options.option_text: ADVISE, the verb 'to give counsel'
ADVICE, the noun 'counsel given'
ADVISES, simple present-tense form
ADVISED, the past-tense form

questions.explanation: ADVICE = NOUN ('a piece of advice'); pronounced /ad-VICE/ (with 's' sound). ADVISE = VERB ('to advise someone'); pronounced /ad-VIZE/ (with 'z' sound). Mnemonic: 'C' for counsel (noun); 'S' for suggest (verb). Same pattern: PRACTICE (noun) / PRACTISE (verb in British English; US uses 'practice' for both). Similar: DEVICE (noun) / DEVISE (verb); LICENCE (noun, BrE) / LICENSE (verb).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The ___ of his speech was peace.' (principle / principal)

options.option_text: PRINCIPAL, meaning 'main / chief'
PRINCIPLE, meaning 'rule, doctrine'
PRINCIPALS, the plural of head
PRINCIPLED, having strong principles

questions.explanation: PRINCIPLE (noun) = a fundamental rule, doctrine, or theme. PRINCIPAL (noun) = head of a school / institution; or (adj) = main, primary. Mnemonic: 'priniciPAL is your PAL (the school head)'; 'principLE = LE for rule'. SSC PYQ favorite. Examples: 'principles of chemistry' (rules); 'principal of college' (head); 'principal cause' (main cause).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The weather had a great ___ on the crops.' (effect / affect)

options.option_text: AFFECT, the verb 'to influence'
EFFECT, the noun 'a result'
AFFECTS, plural form of verb
AFFECTED, past tense of affect

questions.explanation: EFFECT (noun) = a result, an outcome. AFFECT (verb) = to influence, to have an impact on. Mnemonic: 'A' for Action (verb), 'E' for End-result (noun). Examples: 'Smoking AFFECTS health' (verb); 'The EFFECT of smoking is bad' (noun). Trickier: 'EFFECT' as verb = to bring about ('she effected change' = caused). 'AFFECT' as noun (psychology) = emotional response — rare usage.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'They made ___ at the breakfast table.' (peace / piece)

options.option_text: PIECE, meaning 'a portion of'
PEACE, meaning 'tranquility / calm'
PIECES, the plural form here
PEACEFUL, the adjective form

questions.explanation: PEACE = freedom from war / tranquility / agreement (made peace = settled their differences). PIECE = a portion of something; a part. Mnemonic: 'piEce' has 'E' = 'a piece of pie' (food, part); 'pEAce' has 'EA' = 'pEAce on EArth'. SSC PYQ word-pair. 'They made PIECES at table' would mean broke things into bits (different).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Please ___ your seat-belt before takeoff.' (fasten / fastening)

options.option_text: FASTENING — gerund/continuous form
FASTEN — base infinitive after 'please'
FASTENS — third-person present
FASTENED — past tense of fasten

questions.explanation: Imperative form (command/request) takes the BASE form of the verb: 'Please fasten...'. 'T' is silent in 'fasten' /FAS-en/ — like 'listen', 'often', 'soften', 'castle'. Common SSC trick — testing imperative + silent letters. Distractor 1 — gerund needs 'be' (are fastening). Distractor 3 — needs subject. Distractor 4 — past tense doesn't fit imperative.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'I cannot ___ his bad behaviour anymore.' (bear / bare)

options.option_text: BARE, meaning 'naked / uncovered'
BEAR, meaning 'to tolerate / endure'
BORE, the past-tense form here
BORN, past participle of bear

questions.explanation: BEAR (verb) = to tolerate, endure; also a noun (the animal); also = to carry, give birth ('she bore a son'). BARE (adj) = naked, uncovered ('bare hands', 'bare-foot'). 'Cannot BEAR' = cannot tolerate — common idiom. Distractor 1 — BARE doesn't fit context. Distractor 3 — past tense, present continuous needed. Distractor 4 — different sense.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Take care of your ___ and the pounds will take care of themselves.' (cents / sense)

options.option_text: SENSE, meaning 'good judgement'
PENCE / CENTS, the small currency
SCENTS, fragrances or perfumes only
SENSES, the plural form noun

questions.explanation: Famous saying — 'take care of the PENCE (or CENTS) and the pounds (or dollars) will take care of themselves' (origin: William Lowndes, 18th c., variously attributed). Means: small savings add up. Pence/cents = small currency units; pounds/dollars = larger units. Distractor 1 SENSE = judgement, doesn't fit. Distractor 3 SCENTS = fragrances, wrong context. Common SSC PYQ idiom test.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The office manager placed an order for ___ including ruled notebooks, sketch pens, and file folders.

options.option_text: stationary — remaining fixed without any movement
stationery — paper, pens, and other office supplies
stationer — a retail dealer in writing materials
stationed — posted at a particular official location

questions.explanation: 'Stationery' (noun) refers to writing and office materials. 'Stationary' (adjective, the tempting distractor) means not moving. A reliable memory aid: 'stationEry' contains 'E' for papEr. 'Stationer' is a dealer in such supplies, not the supplies themselves.

questions.stem: The tangy mango chutney was the ideal ___ to the spicy biryani served at the feast.

options.option_text: compliment — a remark that expresses admiration
complement — something that completes or enhances
complimentary — offered without any charge as a gesture
supplementary — added as an extra or additional part

questions.explanation: 'Complement' means something that completes or perfectly enhances another thing. 'Compliment' (the most tempting distractor) means a flattering remark. The sentence describes the chutney enhancing the biryani, not praising it, so 'complement' is correct.

questions.stem: The pyrotechnician fired a ___ into the sky to signal the rescue team waiting in the dense fog.

options.option_text: flair — expressing natural talent in a stylish way
flare — a bright burst of light or signal device
flairs — plural for natural abilities and panache
flared — widened outward gradually at the bottom

questions.explanation: 'Flare' refers to a bright burst of light or a pyrotechnic signalling device, fitting the rescue context precisely. 'Flair' (the tempting distractor) means a natural talent or stylish quality, which has no connection to signalling through fog.

questions.stem: The Himalayan expedition team celebrated its successful ___ to the summit after three weeks of gruelling trekking.

options.option_text: absent — not present or missing from the venue
accent — a distinctive manner of pronunciation
assent — agreement or formal approval given willingly
ascent — an upward climb or rise to a summit

questions.explanation: 'Ascent' means an upward journey or physical climb to a higher point. 'Assent' (the most tempting distractor, as it is a near-homophone) means formal agreement or approval. The expedition-to-summit context signals a physical upward climb, not an approval or consent.

questions.stem: The architect submitted detailed blueprints for the construction ___ located adjacent to the heritage corridor.

options.option_text: sight — the faculty of perceiving using the eyes
cite — to quote from an authoritative source text
site — a specific place designated for a purpose
sighted — possessing the full ability to see clearly

questions.explanation: 'Site' means a location designated for a specific activity such as construction. 'Sight' (vision) is the most frequent distractor because it is a perfect homophone. 'Cite' means to reference a source. The blueprint-and-construction context uniquely points to 'site'.

questions.stem: The documentary filmmaker used candid, informal conversations to ___ genuine emotional responses from the survivors of the flood.

options.option_text: illicit — unlawful or morally forbidden by social norms
solicit — to approach someone formally and ask a favour
elicit — to draw out or evoke a particular reaction
explicit — expressed in a fully clear and direct manner

questions.explanation: 'Elicit' means to draw out or evoke a response. 'Illicit' (the primary homophone distractor) means unlawful — same pronunciation but entirely opposite meaning. 'Solicit' tempts because it involves requesting something, but it carries a formal or transactional connotation unlike the candid indirect method described in the stem.

questions.stem: The seismology department issued a bulletin warning that a powerful aftershock was ___ and urged coastal communities to move to higher ground.

options.option_text: eminent — widely respected and distinguished by merit
immanent — inherently present within a system or entity
imminent — certain to happen very soon or at any moment
prominent — easily noticed or standing out conspicuously

questions.explanation: 'Imminent' means about to happen in the very near future, precisely fitting a seismic warning requiring evacuation. 'Eminent' (confused due to similar pronunciation) means famous or distinguished — the most common mix-up in exams. 'Immanent' is a philosophical term meaning inherently present within something and is unrelated to time; 'prominent' means standing out noticeably.
